CBS News live

Updated on:  November 4, 2026 / 2:38 AM EST
            / CBS News

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race, CBS News projects, becoming the nation's first Muslim senator and retaining the seat for Democrats after one of the most contentious contests of the midterm elections.

His win came after a last-minute shakeup in the race, with former Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens endorsing Rogers over the weekend.

In his first public comments since Democrats notched House and Senate victories, billionaire Elon Musk wrote on X: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."

The world's richest man spent hundreds of millions of dollars assisting Republican congressional candidates. His biggest investment came in the Texas Senate race, which Republican Ken Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico.

Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932 on Tuesday — a feat that required him to convince a large number of Republicans to cross the aisle and vote for him, even if that meant losing the Senate majority for their preferred party.

CBS News asked what he thinks Democrats should do first. He said they should end the war in Iran, address tariffs, lower healthcare costs and restore programs like SNAP — commonly known as food stamps — that were curtailed by the last Congress.

When asked what Democrats could propose that he wouldn't support on behalf of the Republicans who voted for him, he said he believed in a strong border.

"I am an independent-minded Democrat. I'm going to work across the aisle so that Republicans and Democrats take into account each other's concerns," he told CBS News.

Hamilton now has the task of representing his bipartisan coalition in a Congress where Democrats have been empowered with control of both houses. Kansas' other Senate seat is held by Republican Sen. Jerry Moran, who Hamilton has said will be his "best friend."

"We are not flyover country. We are the heart of America. And today the heart of America has sent Washington a message: that we are better together than we are divided," Hamilton told supporters in a victory speech.

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took the stage in Michigan to declare victory. CBS News has not projected a winner in the race, which remains tight, though Democrats are assessed as the likely winners.

"Michigan, we did it!" El-Sayed said.

He said he is "so proud and honored" to be their senator-elect. If he wins against Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed will be the first Muslim-American elected to the U.S. Senate.

"You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates, so thank you," he said. "This is all yours."

He thanked voters for inviting him to their churches, synagogues and homes.

"Thank you for your trust and your belief and your kindness," he said. "I'm going to take it all with me and I hope to bring back the kind of leadership that more than earns it."

El-Sayed said his opponents weren't just targeting and attacking him, "they were targeting and attacking you."

"They want an America that is too small for some of us. We know that America is big enough for all of us," he said.

It was a bitter race. El-Sayed's vehement criticism of the Israeli government drew stiff pushback from Republicans and some moderate Democrats in both the primary and general election, and President Trump frequently made incendiary comments about El-Sayed, calling him "Mohammad" and saying he should be forced to go through a metal detector. He pointed to that bitterness during his speech early Wednesday.

"So Mike, enjoy your retirement!" El-Sayed said, telling him to enjoy his yachts.

"You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," he said. "May we never have to see the likes of you in the state again."

"JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January," he said, before nodding to Vice President JD Vance's Ohio heritage. "So you know what that means! Wolverine one, buckeye zero!"

"Donald, look, I know you've struggled with my name," he said. "So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator."

"To the super PACs and special interests who tried to beat us, we are coming for your system of politics," he said. "To AIPAC, who spent $42 million against us, thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice."

Former President Barack Obama said American voters sent a "clear message," but Democrats now need to "roll up our sleeves."

"Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face," said the former president, who held several rallies for Democratic candidates in recent weeks.

"These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country — including in areas once considered long shots," he said. "They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first."

He also expressed gratitude to election officials and volunteers.

"While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future," he said.

Embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller lost his bid for reelection to Democrat Brian Poindexter in Ohio's 7th Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Miller defied calls over the summer to end his campaign before a deadline that would have allowed Republicans to replace him on the November ballot amid allegations of domestic abuse toward his ex-wife and young daughter. The allegations, which Miller denied, put the northeastern Ohio district long held by Republicans in play.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the race as solid Republican earlier this year, but shifted the contest to a toss-up in August.

Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is in an unexpectedly close fight to keep her Senate seat. She and Democrat Scott Colom are neck-and-neck in Mississippi, with nearly all of the votes in.

When Republican Sen. Susan Collins was reelected in 2020, she narrowly won women voters. But exit polls show that on Tuesday, they backed Democrat Troy Jackson, who is projected to defeat Collins.

While Collins often tries to distance herself from President Trump, women voters and most Maine voters overall said she was too supportive of the president.

And Mr. Trump's tariffs are not popular here. Most Maine voters (69%) feel they have harmed their local economy. Many in the state said the cost of living was a crucial factor in their vote and they voted for Jackson by a 33-point margin.

Even though more voters thought Collins would do a better job than Jackson getting federal funding for Maine, that wasn't enough to push her over the top.

Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers expressed confidence, telling supporters early Wednesday morning, "there is a path for us to win this thing."

"Guess what's left? It's coming our way," he said.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed currently has a lead, but around one-third of the vote is still uncounted. CBS News assesses that the seat is a likely Democratic win, but has not projected a winner.

Rogers said: "We're very, very confident we're going to turn this thing around," before telling supporters to get some sleep.

Polls closed in Alaska at 1 a.m. ET, meaning all voting in the United States has concluded.

The Senate race in Alaska will be closely watched, by anyone still awake.

In his victory speech in Texas, Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico compared his victory and his story to the biblical story of David and Goliath.
